facts.claim: Smartraveller's overall advice for Nigeria is 'Reconsider your need to travel', including Abuja (as at November 2026; page updated 23 October 2026, still current at 9 November 2026).
facts.quote: Reconsider your need to travel to Nigeria overall, including the capital Abuja, due to the volatile security situation and threat of terrorism, kidnapping, violent crime and the risk of civil unrest.

facts.claim: Smartraveller lists 26 states plus the Federal Capital Territory (excluding Abuja) at 'Do not travel', as published: Abia, Adamawa, Anambra, Akawa Ibom, Bauchi, Bayelsa, Borno, Cross Rivers, Delta, Enugu, FCT (excluding Abuja), Gombe, Imo, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Kogi, Kwara, Niger, Plateau, Rivers, Sokoto, Taraba, Yobe, Zamfara.
facts.quote: Do not travel to: Abia Adamawa Anambra Akawa Ibom Bauchi Bayelsa Borno Cross Rivers Delta Enugu Federal Capital Territory (excluding Abuja) Gombe Imo Jigawa Kaduna Kano Katsina Kebbi Kogi Kwara Niger Plateau Rivers Sokoto Taraba Yobe Zamfara states due to the volatile security situation...
facts.conflicts: Page spells 'Akawa Ibom' and 'Cross Rivers'; correct names are Akwa Ibom and Cross River. If quoting, use page wording or list the correct state names without quotation marks.

facts.claim: Smartraveller: Nigeria has strict laws against same-sex relationships; the Australian High Commission in Abuja and the Honorary Consulate in Lagos provide limited consular and passport services.
facts.quote: Nigeria has strict laws against same-sex relationships. ... The Australian High Commission in Abuja and Australia's Honorary Consulate in Lagos provide limited consular and passport services.

facts.claim: The Australian High Commission in Nigeria (Abuja) home page is live (HTTP 200) and gives urgent consular contacts during business hours, with the 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre in Canberra (+61 2 6261 3305; 1300 555 135 within Australia) at other times.
facts.quote: If you are an Australian in need of urgent consular assistance please contact: During business hours (0800-1630 Monday to Thursday and 0800-1230 on Friday) the Australian High Commission in Nigeria ... At all other times please contact the Consular Emergency Centre (CEC).

facts.claim: Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18 August 2026): an overseas marriage cannot be registered in Australia but in most cases is legally recognised if it was valid where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law; it advises talking to a lawyer.
facts.quote: You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia. But in most cases, your marriage is legally recognised here. To be recognised, when you got married it must have been: valid under the law of the country where it happened; valid under Australian law if it had occurred in Australia.

facts.claim: UNESCO's Nigeria page (live, title 'Nigeria - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage') lists 8 inscribed elements: Durbar in Kano (2024), Midwifery (2023, multinational), Sango Festival, Oyo (2023), Kwagh-Hir theatrical performance (2019), Argungu international fishing and cultural festival (2016), Ijele masquerade (2009), Oral heritage of Gelede (2008), Ifa divination system (2008). No listed title names weddings or marriage; element pages were not read (a guessed Ijele URL redirected to an unrelated Chinese element). UNESCO should be omitted from the copy.
facts.quote: 8 elements inscribed ... 2024: Durbar in Kano (RL) ... 2009: Ijele masquerade (RL) 2008: Oral heritage of Gelede (RL) 2008: Ifa divination system (RL)

facts.claim: Britannica: the Igbo live chiefly in southeastern Nigeria, number more than 35 million (2020s estimate), are widely dispersed within Nigeria and across many countries, and many are now Christians. The article does not describe marriage customs.
facts.quote: Igbo, people living chiefly in southeastern Nigeria ... They are widely dispersed within Nigeria and across many different countries throughout the world. ... Many Igbo are now Christians

facts.claim: An academic study of Igbo marriage in Ezinifite-Aguata (Anambra State) describes five stages: knocking at the door (Ịkụ aka n'ụzọ), presentation of gifts (Ịgbanye ihe), outing ceremony (Ịkpọta nwaanyị), paying of bride price (Ime ego) and the public traditional marriage ceremony (Ịgba mmanya ọha niile), with palm wine used to communicate at each stage. Tone-marked terms as the source gives them; the author notes palm wine customs differ between Igbo communities.
facts.quote: there are five stages involved in the process of marriage in Ezinifite-Aguata. The first stage is knocking at the door (Ịkụ aka n'ụzọ), ... fourth is paying of bride price (Ime ego), and the fifth is the traditional marriage ceremony (Ịgba mmanya ọha niile). At each stage, communication is carried out through palm wine.
facts.note: Umezi, P. I. (2026) 'Communicative Competence of Palm Wine in Igbo Traditional Marriage Process in Ezinifite-Aguata', International Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities Review 16(4): 57-68 (Nnamdi Azikiwe University), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

facts.claim: Knocking at the door is the first stage 'in Ezinifite-Aguata and most of the communities in Igboland': the suitor and his father visit the woman's family with palm wine to register interest; the hosts present kola nut as a sign of welcome; the daughter is given a cup of palm wine and, if she consents, sips it and hands the rest to her suitor.
facts.quote: the suitor and his father would approach the family of the proposed wife with two gallons (ten litters) of palm wine to register their interest in the marriage. This is the first introduction. On their arrival, the host family would present kola nut to the guests as a sign of welcome. ... She would sip and give the remaining to the fiancé, if she wish to consent to the marriage.
facts.note: Describes Ezinifite-Aguata; 'most of the communities in Igboland' for the first stage. Do not state quantities of palm wine in copy.

facts.claim: At the bride price stage (ime ego), the groom's kinsmen accompany him to the bride's family; after kola nut and palm wine, he offers the bride price to his father-in-law, who in the study's account takes part and returns the rest, saying he is not selling his daughter; other items for the ceremony are then presented. No amounts.
facts.quote: the in-law would accept the offer, take some amount and give the rest back to his in-law, saying: “I am not selling my daughter to you; but take her as your help mate.” After that, other items for the inner traditional marriage ceremony would be presented.
facts.note: Community-specific; write as 'in some Igbo communities'. No amounts.

facts.claim: At the public traditional marriage ceremony, the bride's father pours her a cup of palm wine and asks her to show the gathering her husband ('gosi anyị onye bụ di gị'); she sips it, walks through the guests in search of the groom, offers him the wine, he drinks it, and they return the cup to her father together. Eating, drinking, dancing and gifts to the couple follow.
facts.quote: The father of the bride would pour a cup of palm wine and give to her daughter saying in a low tone, “gosi anyị onye bụ di gị” (show us who is your husband). She would sip it as usual and walk through the gathering in search of the groom. When she found him, she would offer him the wine. ... After this ceremony, people can now eat, drink and dance. Some would present different gifts to the new couple.
facts.note: The study names this stage Ịgba mmanya ọha niile; 'igba nkwu' is not the term used in this source. The study also says money is placed in the cup: do not mention amounts.

facts.claim: In the same study, at the gift-presentation and outing stages the bride-to-be hands the palm wine to her fiancé while kneeling on one knee as a sign of respect, signalling public acceptance.
facts.quote: She would sip the wine and give the remaining to her fiancé while kneeling before him with one of her knees as a sign of respect. ... The fiancée giving the wine to the fiancé indicates her public acceptance of the offer of marriage.

facts.claim: At the public ceremony the groom's palm wine is examined by the bride's father and kinsmen, and the married daughters of the kindred (ụmụada) and young daughters (ụmụagbọghọ) ask for their entitlements before the ceremony begins: a sourced basis for 'the bride's kin have their own requests' (items, no amounts).
facts.quote: They would examine both the quantity and the quality of the wine. Other groups like the married daughters of the kindred (ụmụada) and the young daughters of the kindred (ụmụagbọghọ) would demand for their entitlements. If they certify everything, the official ceremony would commence.

facts.claim: The study describes palm wine as central to any Igbo traditional ceremony and the preferred drink at weddings, child naming ceremonies, funerals and memorials.
facts.quote: We cannot talk of Igbo culture and tradition without making reference to palm wine. It is a central drink in any Igbo traditional ceremony. ... In every traditional ceremony be it wedding, child naming ceremony, funeral or memorial, palm wine is the preferred drink.

insider_details.detail: Smartraveller's 'Do not travel' list includes Abia, Anambra, Enugu and Imo, so Igbo-heritage couples whose families would travel to the south-east for an introduction should take that into account; the customs travel well to a celebration in Australia instead.

Igbo marriage often runs in stages over weeks or months, so a diaspora couple can plan the knocking-on-the-door visit and the bride price at family level well before the big public day, and brief the planner on which stages need a venue.

For the wine-carrying moment, leave clear floor space and a clear path through the guests, with time on the run sheet for the bride to search the room, kneel, and return the cup to her father with the groom before dancing starts.
Palm wine is central to Igbo ceremonies, so ask the venue early about bringing in or serving it, and about corkage, as a booking question.

If any part of the marriage takes place overseas, recognition in Australia depends on validity where it happened and under Australian law: phrase it as a question for a lawyer or your celebrant, never advice.
